1.pericope_label: The bones brought out of their graves and spread before the host of heaven, and death chosen rather than life
debates: Which destruction of the city is meant
Whether the priests and prophets named are the true or the false
Whether the third verse states a punishment or a reason for one
outliers: Ellicott fixes the passage to the Chaldean destruction as continuous with what precedes, where Gill allows the Roman destruction as well
Gill reports the Greek reading that makes the choice of death a reason for the judgment, and Calvin says those who take it so have missed the design of the passage
themes: A judgment that reaches past the moment of death
Stars called as witnesses against those who worshipped them
Idolatry described in the language of adultery
Survivors counted worse off than the slain

4.pericope_label: Shall they fall and not arise: the stork knoweth her appointed times, but my people know not the judgment of the Lord
debates: Whether the fourth verse speaks of men in general or of the Jews
Who speaks the words I hearkened and heard
What the deceit is that they hold fast
outliers: Calvin sets out four ways of construing the fourth verse, including two that make God the one who turns or returns, before taking it as a general maxim
Gill reports a rendering that makes Jerusalem the subject and the people the object of the turning, against the received construction
themes: An argument from what any traveller would do
A word repeated to mark a turning that never turns back
Repentance said to require terror and not only shame
Migrating birds set as a reproach to a settled people

8.pericope_label: How do ye say, We are wise: the pen of the scribes is in vain, and the wise men are ashamed and taken
debates: Whom the reproach is addressed to
What the vanity of the pen of the scribes means
Whether the shame of the wise men is a present fact or a coming punishment
outliers: Clarke takes the clause about the pen to mean that the scribes wrote falsehoods into the text knowingly, where Ellicott reads it of emptying the Law of its meaning by sophistry and Calvin of a Law written to no purpose in such lives
Calvin sets aside the general opinion of interpreters that the reproach is aimed at the priests and chiefs, and extends it to the whole nation
themes: A boast of wisdom answered from the habits of birds
A pen described as lying
Wise men taken like birds in a snare
Shame promised to men who cannot yet blush

10.pericope_label: I will give their wives unto others: they have healed the hurt of my people slightly, saying Peace, peace
debates: Why the passage repeats an earlier discourse
What the word for those who take the fields implies
Whether the want of shame is met by argument or by suffering
outliers: Calvin sorts the chapter into two parties, making the wise men shamed in the ninth verse the deluded people and the shameless of the twelfth their priests and prophets
themes: A warning repeated because it was not felt the first time
Inheritors rather than plunderers named, to fix the loss as permanent
Physicians who plaster over a wound
Impunity inferred from the company one keeps

13.pericope_label: I will surely consume them: no grapes on the vine, and we looked for peace but no good came
debates: Whether the empty vine describes the sin of the people or their punishment
What the closing clause of the thirteenth verse means
Who speaks the cry about entering the fortified cities
outliers: Ellicott prefers the rendering that makes the closing clause of the thirteenth verse mean the law they transgressed, and Calvin says that reference cannot suit the passage at all
Ellicott takes the empty vine for the state of the nation itself rather than a judgment on it, where Henry knows that reading and prefers to make it the judgment
themes: A verb that means gathering and destroying at once
Gifts held on a condition that failed
A flight to strong walls that ends in silence
Hope traced back to the men who supplied it

16.pericope_label: The snorting of his horses heard from Dan, and serpents sent among them that will not be charmed
debates: Whose horses are meant
Whether the sound is heard as far as Jerusalem or only on the frontier
Whether the charming of serpents is a real practice or a common belief
outliers: Calvin refers the horses to God as the first mover of the war, where Gill makes them the horses of Nebuchadnezzar and reports the other view as Calvin own
Ellicott treats serpent-charming as a real and ancient practice, where Calvin says the prophet does not vouch for it but speaks according to the common opinion of men
themes: A war already at the border while the capital sits easy
A patristic reading dismissed as an eccentricity
An enemy figured as a snake that cannot be charmed
Diplomacy compared to an incantation

18.pericope_label: When I would comfort myself my heart is faint: is not the Lord in Zion, and the harvest is past
debates: What the word rendered comfort means
Whose heart faints in the eighteenth verse
What the passing of harvest and summer refers to
outliers: Wesley and Gill take the fainting heart for the prophet in sympathy with his people, where Calvin denies it can be the prophet at all and makes it the obstinacy of the people
Ellicott reads the passing of harvest as a failure of crops, Clarke as two years of siege, and Calvin as the season for an ally to march
themes: A word that occurs once and cannot be fixed
A prophet speaking three parts in one verse
A question answered by another question
A proverb of hope that ran out of season

21.pericope_label: For the hurt of my people am I hurt: is there no balm in Gilead, is there no physician there
debates: Who speaks the lament of the twenty-first verse
What the balm of Gilead was
Whether the closing questions are to be answered yes or no
outliers: Clarke answers both closing questions in the affirmative and makes the failure the fault of the patient, where Calvin makes them a declaration that the disease was incurable and every remedy vain
Gill and Calvin both reject the rendering treacle as absurd, treacle being a compound where the word means a single gum
themes: A prophet mocked for grieving over other men trouble
A remedy named for the country that produced it best
Physicians identified with the prophets themselves
Questions that may be a reproach or a verdict
